articleSummary: XFG, a SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariant, is driving the current rise in COVID-19 cases globally. First detected January 2025; by June 2025 it surpassed B.1.8.1 to become the dominant global lineage, and the October 4 update showed XFG at 52% of sequences. In Brazil, it was officially confirmed in July 2025 and has since been the main circulating variant, at times nearly 100% of sequenced samples; this year XFG accounts for about 90% of 2,199 analyzed Brazilian cases. The WHO states there is no evidence of greater severity than other Omicron descendants, and vaccines plus prior infection continue to protect against severe disease. The subvariant carries spike mutations with potential immune escape and higher transmissibility. Through November 4, 2026, Brazil reported 118,851 COVID-19–related respiratory illness cases, with rising activity across multiple states (Alagoas, Bahia, Ceará, Distrito Federal, Espírito Santo, Goiás, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso, Paraíba, Pernambuco, Piauí, Paraná, Rio de Janeiro, Rondônia, Roraima, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, São Paulo); ITPS positivity rose from 6.62% to 16.66% last week. In 2025 mid-Oct, 367,640 cases were reported; this year 115,626 (−68.5%).

articleHeadline: 登革熱有解？野放「帶菌斑蚊」4年 染疫風險大減近7成
articleSummary: Four-year follow-up in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, involving over 5,700 children, shows a Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti release markedly lowers dengue fever and chikungunya infections by about 69%. The World Mosquito Program inserts Wolbachia bacteria into mosquitoes to reduce their ability to transmit viruses; infected mosquitoes pass the bacteria to offspring, enabling the virus-blocking effect to spread as the population grows. Compared with matched control areas, the intervention’s protective impact persisted even during Brazil’s severe dengue outbreak in 2024. In communities with standard insecticide spraying, half were randomly selected to receive Wolbachia releases, confirming effectiveness against dengue and chikungunya. Zika virus cases were too few to assess. Experts suggest integrating Wolbachia with existing vector-control measures could push dengue incidence to new lows.
